Wendy's rejected an offer from billionaire Nelson Peltz's hedge fund Trian Fund Partners to take the fast food chain private for $1.4 billion, telling investors the deal "substantially" undervalued the company, which has posted same-store sales declines for seven straight quarters.

The fast food burger chain has struggled in recent years, posting seven straight quarters of declining same-store sales.

Trian proposed a deal to take Wendy's private last week, alongside Flynn Group, BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners, offering to buy all outstanding shares for $7.35 in cash—representing a roughly 20% premium on the company's share price at the time the deal was announced.

Wendy's rejected Trian's offer on Thursday after an independent committee reviewed the plan and "unanimously concluded" it undervalued the fast food chain, Wendy's chairman Art Winkleblack said in a press release on Thursday, specifically the company's "standalone prospects and long-term earnings potential."

Winkleblack said the company's board still had confidence in the leadership of president and CEO Bob Wright, who he said had a "proven track record of seasoned industry leadership."

The company also said it would adopt a shareholder rights plan aimed at preventing an individual investor or group from gaining "actual or negative control," which it said would kick in if an investor owns more than 15% of its stock.

Wendy's was previously the second-largest burger chain in the U.S. in terms of sales, behind only McDonald's. However, the fast food chain, founded by Dave Thomas in 1969, has now posted declining same-store sales for seven straight quarters after releasing third quarter results on Thursday morning. Wright, who took the reins as CEO in May, previously told the Wall Street Journal the company's business was stalling due to "decisions around quality that were rooted in efficiency and cost savings," and said the restaurant was "over-reliant on promotional activity and everyday-value strategies." Instead, Wright said the company would "rebuild" its menu starting with individual ingredients and the Wendy's primary menu offerings. "Hamburgers, chicken, salads—those are the primary categories for us. And desserts led by our Frosty," Wright said.

We estimate Nelson Peltz, an activist investor and the co-founder of Trian, has a net worth of $1.6 billion. Peltz also has a long history with Wendy's—he served as the chairman of the company's board for 17 years, only stepping down in 2024. His son, Bradley Peltz, currently sits on Wendy's board, and has an ownership stake in a Wendy's franchisee that operates 87 restaurants, according to the company. Trian still owns a roughly 16% stake in the fast food company, according to regulatory filings.
